sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06: syllabus and learning goals

lessons.title: Vector arithmetic and linear combinations
lessons.summary: Calculate with coordinates, describe spans, and determine whether a representation is possible and unique.
objectives: Compute coordinatewise vector sums and scalar multiples in a specified real coordinate space.
Solve for the coefficients of a linear combination and recognize vectors outside a span.
Distinguish a unique representation from infinitely many representations using linear independence.

sections.heading: Coordinates encode both direction and magnitude
sections.body: A vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an ordered list of $n$ real numbers. Equality requires equality in every coordinate. Addition and scalar multiplication are coordinatewise: $(u+v)_i=u_i+v_i$ and $(cu)_i=cu_i$. The order of coordinates matters: $(2,5)$ and $(5,2)$ are different vectors. Vectors can describe displacement, holdings, or coefficients; those interpretations do not change the algebra. You may add vectors only when they belong to the same coordinate space.

sections.heading: A span is the set of all reachable combinations
sections.body: A linear combination of $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ is $c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k$, with real coefficients unless another scalar field is specified. Their span consists of every vector obtainable this way. To test whether $b$ lies in the span, equate coordinates and solve all resulting equations together. For instance, the span of $(1,2)$ contains exactly the vectors $(t,2t)$; $(3,6)$ belongs to it, while $(3,7)$ does not. The zero vector always belongs to a span because all coefficients may be zero.

sections.heading: Independence controls uniqueness
sections.body: The vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ are linearly independent when $c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k=0$ forces every coefficient to be zero. If two representations of the same vector existed, subtracting them would give a nonzero coefficient solution to that homogeneous equation. Thus independence gives at most one representation. Dependent vectors can still span useful sets, but coefficients are not unique when a representation exists. Containing a zero vector or containing one vector that is a scalar multiple of another guarantees dependence.

steps: This gives $(-7,7,-8)$; the second coordinate is positive because subtracting $-3$ adds $3$.
For the zero target, the same equations give $a+b_2=0$ and $a-b_2=0$, forcing both coefficients to be zero.
The two generating vectors are independent, so the representation just computed is unique.

questions.prompt: For $u=(2,-1,3)$ and $v=(-1,4,2)$, compute $3u-2v$. Enter the three coordinates.

hints: Add the two equations to eliminate $b$.
questions.solution: Adding $2a-b=1$ and $a+b=5$ gives $3a=6$, so $a=2$. Then $b=5-a=3$. Substitution gives $(4-3,2+3)=(1,5)$.

questions.prompt: Which vector is outside $\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,3),(2,4,6)\}$?
hints: The second generating vector is twice the first.
Every reachable vector has third coordinate three times its first.
questions.solution: The span is the line $(t,2t,3t)$. The first three options have that form, but $(1,2,4)$ would require both $t=1$ and $3t=4$, which is impossible.

questions.prompt: For which real number $t$ does $(4,t)$ belong to the span of $(2,3)$?
questions.solution: The equation $2c=4$ gives $c=2$. The second coordinate must then be $t=3c=6$.

questions.prompt: Express $(-2,7,1)$ in the standard coordinate vectors $e_1,e_2,e_3$. Enter the coefficients in that order.
hints: Each standard vector changes only one coordinate.

questions.prompt: How many pairs $(a,b)$ solve $a(1,2)+b(2,4)=(3,6)$?
hints: The second coordinate equation is twice the first.
questions.solution: Both coordinates reduce to $a+2b=3$. Every real $b$ gives the solution $a=3-2b$, so infinitely many coefficient pairs represent the target.

questions.prompt: Order these steps to prove that independent vectors give unique coefficients in a linear combination.
choices: Independence forces every coefficient $a_i-b_i$ to be zero.
Suppose $\sum_i a_iv_i=\sum_i b_iv_i$ are two representations of the same vector.
Therefore $a_i=b_i$ for every $i$, so the representations agree.
hints: Begin by assuming two representations of one target.
Subtract before invoking the definition of independence.
questions.solution: Assume two representations, subtract them, invoke independence on the resulting zero combination, and conclude equality of every coefficient. The order is $2,4,1,3$.

questions.prompt: Let $v=(3,-1,2)$ and $u=(-2,4,1)$. Solve $x+2v=u$ for the vector $x$.

questions.solution: Substitute $b=2a$ into $a+3b=7$ to get $7a=7$. Thus $a=1$ and $b=2$, and $(1,2)+2(3,-1)=(7,0)$.

questions.prompt: A student claims every vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a combination of $(2,-1)$ and $(-4,2)$. Which target disproves this?
hints: The second generator is $-2$ times the first.
questions.solution: Any combination is $(2a-4b,-a+2b)$ and satisfies $y=-x/2$. The target $(1,0)$ violates that relation. The other three targets lie on the line.

lessons.title: Dot products, norms, and angles
lessons.summary: Measure lengths and angles, detect orthogonality, and separate a vector into parallel and perpendicular components.
objectives: Compute Euclidean dot products, norms, and distances.
Recover an angle or projection from a dot product while handling zero-vector exceptions.
Use orthogonality and Cauchy–Schwarz to justify geometric claims.

sections.heading: The Euclidean dot product
sections.body: For real vectors of the same dimension, $u\cdot v=\sum_i u_iv_i$. The Euclidean norm is $\|u\|=\sqrt{u\cdot u}$, and the distance between $u$ and $v$ is $\|u-v\|$. Length is nonnegative and equals zero exactly for the zero vector. Scaling obeys $\|cu\|=|c|\|u\|$, so a negative scalar reverses direction without making length negative. Do not confuse the scalar $u\cdot v$ with a vector.

sections.heading: Angles and orthogonality
sections.body: For nonzero vectors, $u\cdot v=\|u\|\|v\|\cos\theta$, with $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$. The sign of the dot product identifies an acute, right, or obtuse angle. Nonzero perpendicular vectors have dot product zero; the zero vector is algebraically orthogonal to every vector but has no defined direction or angle. Cauchy–Schwarz, $|u\cdot v|\leq\|u\|\|v\|$, ensures the cosine quotient is within $[-1,1]$. Equality holds when the vectors are dependent.

sections.heading: Projection gives a best parallel approximation
sections.body: For a nonzero vector $a$, the component of $v$ along its line is $p=((v\cdot a)/(a\cdot a))a$. Derive this by writing $p=ca$ and imposing $(v-ca)\cdot a=0$, which gives $c=(v\cdot a)/(a\cdot a)$. The residual $r=v-p$ is perpendicular to $a$. For any other point $ta$ on the line, $\|v-ta\|^2=\|r\|^2+\|p-ta\|^2$, so the projection uniquely minimizes distance to the line.

steps: Both norms are $\sqrt{2}$, so neither vector is zero.
worked_examples.result: The angle is $90$ degrees, and the vectors are perpendicular.

worked_examples.prompt: Project $v=(3,4)$ onto the line generated by $a=(1,2)$.
worked_examples.result: $p=(2.2,4.4)$ is the unique nearest point on the line.

questions.prompt: Find the Euclidean norm of $(2,-3,6)$.
Find the distance between $(1,-2)$ and $(4,2)$.
Choose $k$ so that $(1,k,2)$ and $(3,2,-1)$ are perpendicular.
questions.solution: The dot product is $1+2k$. Setting it to zero gives $k=-1/2$.

questions.prompt: What is the angle, in degrees, between $(1,0)$ and $(1,\sqrt{3})$?
hints: The dot product is $1$ and the norms are $1$ and $2$.
questions.solution: $\cos\theta=1/(1\cdot2)=1/2$, so the angle is $60$ degrees.

questions.prompt: Project $(2,3)$ onto the line spanned by $(1,1)$. Enter the projected vector.
hints: The numerator is $5$ and denominator is $2$.
questions.solution: The projection coefficient is $5/2$, so $p=(5/2)(1,1)=(2.5,2.5)$. The residual $(-0.5,0.5)$ is perpendicular to $(1,1)$.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly handles the zero vector?
choices: Its angle with every nonzero vector is zero.
It is orthogonal to every vector, but its angle with a nonzero vector is undefined.
Its norm is one because it has no direction.
Its angle with every vector is ninety degrees by the cosine formula.
questions.answer: It is orthogonal to every vector, but its angle with a nonzero vector is undefined.
hints: The dot product with zero is always zero.
The angle formula would divide by a zero norm.
questions.solution: Algebraic orthogonality means zero dot product, so zero is orthogonal to every vector. The angle formula requires both norms to be nonzero, so it cannot assign a direction or angle to zero.

questions.prompt: Order the steps deriving the coefficient of the orthogonal projection of $v$ onto the span of nonzero $a$.
choices: Solve for $c=(v\cdot a)/(a\cdot a)$ because $a\cdot a>0$.
hints: First parameterize a vector on the line.
Expand the perpendicularity condition before dividing.
questions.solution: Write $p=ca$, require $v-p$ to be perpendicular to $a$, expand the dot product, and divide by the positive number $a\cdot a$. The sequence is $2,3,4,1$.

questions.prompt: Let $p$ be the projection of $v=(4,1)$ onto the span of $a=(2,-1)$. Compute the residual $v-p$.
For which pair does equality hold in $|u\cdot v|\leq\|u\|\|v\|$?
hints: A negative scalar multiple still gives equality because the dot product is inside absolute values.
questions.solution: Here $v=-3u$, so $|u\cdot v|=15$ and $\|u\|\|v\|=\sqrt5(3\sqrt5)=15$. None of the other pairs is proportional.

lessons.title: Matrix arithmetic
lessons.summary: Use dimensions and row-column products to calculate sums, products, and transposes, and identify where scalar intuitions fail.
objectives: Determine when a matrix sum or product exists and compute its dimensions.
Calculate matrix products and connect them to columns and composition.
Use transpose identities and counterexamples to reject false matrix algebra rules.

sections.heading: Shape determines which operations exist
sections.body: An $m\times n$ matrix has $m$ rows and $n$ columns. Addition is entrywise and requires the same shape; scalar multiplication changes every entry. If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $AB$ is $m\times p$. The matching inner dimension $n$ counts the terms in each row-column dot product. The product can be valid even when $BA$ is undefined. A zero matrix has a shape, so a rectangular zero matrix cannot simply be substituted for any other zero matrix.

sections.heading: Multiplication combines rows with columns
sections.body: The entry $(AB)_{ij}$ is $\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}B_{kj}$. Equivalently, column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$. These descriptions prevent the common error of multiplying corresponding entries. Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive when dimensions match, but generally not commutative. For example, a shear followed by a stretch can give a different map from the stretch followed by the shear. The identity matrix satisfies $I_mA=A=AI_n$ for $A$ of shape $m\times n$.

sections.heading: Transpose reverses multiplication order
sections.body: The transpose interchanges rows and columns: $(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji}$. It satisfies $(A+B)^T=A^T+B^T$ and $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$. To see why the latter reverses order, the $(i,j)$ entry of $(AB)^T$ is $\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}$, which is the $(i,j)$ entry of $B^TA^T$. Shape checking is an independent audit: if $AB$ is $m\times p$, both transposed expressions must be $p\times m$. Unlike real numbers, nonzero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix, so cancellation needs additional hypotheses.

steps: Both factors are $2\times2$, so the product is $2\times2$.
Thus $AB=\begin{pmatrix}4&8\\1&12\end{pmatrix}$. Its first column also equals $A(2,1)=(4,1)$.
Multiplying in the reverse order gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
The upper-right entries differ, so the two products are unequal.
Applying the products to $e_2=(0,1)$ gives $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$, an explicit vector witnessing the difference.
worked_examples.result: $AB\ne BA$ even though both products exist.

questions.prompt: $A$ is $3\times2$ and $B$ is $2\times4$. What is the shape of $AB$?
hints: The outer dimensions give rows and columns of the result.
questions.solution: The shared dimension is $2$. Each of the $3$ rows of $A$ pairs with each of the $4$ columns of $B$, giving a $3\times4$ product.

questions.prompt: Compute $2A-B$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.solution: $2A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-4\\6&0\end{pmatrix}$. Entrywise subtraction gives $\begin{pmatrix}2-4&-4-1\\6-(-1)&0-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-5\\7&-2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: Compute $AB$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: Each product entry is a row-column dot product.
questions.solution: The four entries are $2+0=2$, $-1+6=5$, $6+0=6$, and $-3+12=9$. Hence $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\6&9\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: Compute $Ax$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&3\\0&4&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=(2,1,-1)$.
hints: The $2\times3$ matrix maps a three-coordinate vector to two coordinates.
questions.solution: The first coordinate is $1(2)-2(1)+3(-1)=-3$ and the second is $0(2)+4(1)-1(-1)=5$. Thus $Ax=(-3,5)$.

questions.prompt: Transpose $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\-1&0&4\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: The result has three rows and two columns.
questions.solution: The first row $(1,2,3)$ becomes the first column, and the second row $(-1,0,4)$ becomes the second column. Thus $A^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\2&0\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: For compatible real matrices $A,B$, which identity is always valid?
hints: Transposition reverses the order of a product.
A nonzero strictly upper-triangular $2\times2$ matrix can square to zero.
questions.solution: The row-column definition gives $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$. Commutativity fails in general, and $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is nonzero but has square zero.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-1\\0&3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-2&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Find entry $(1,2)$ of $AB$ (indices start at $1$).
hints: Use row $1$ of $A$ and column $2$ of $B$.

questions.prompt: Suppose $A$ is $2\times3$ and $B$ is $3\times4$. Which statement is correct?
choices: Neither product exists because $A$ and $B$ have different shapes.
hints: Check inner dimensions separately for each order.
questions.solution: $AB$ has matching inner dimension $3$ and shape $2\times4$. For $BA$, the inner dimensions are $4$ and $2$, so the product is undefined.

questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, compute $AB-BA$.
questions.solution: $AB=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting yields $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $(AB)^T$.
hints: Interchange rows and columns, or use $B^TA^T$.
questions.solution: Multiplication gives $AB=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$. Its transpose is $\begin{pmatrix}5&-1\\4&-2\end{pmatrix}$, also obtained from $B^TA^T$.

lessons.title: Linear transformations in coordinates
lessons.summary: Build a matrix from basis-vector images and interpret matrix multiplication as composition of linear maps.
objectives: Test the two linearity properties and use an explicit counterexample when they fail.
Recover the standard matrix of a linear map from its values on basis vectors.
Compute compositions and identify simple kernels and images.

sections.heading: Linearity is a statement about every input
sections.body: A map $T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is linear if $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ and $T(cu)=cT(u)$ for every $u,v$ and real $c$. Equivalently, $T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$. Every linear map satisfies $T(0)=0$, but that condition alone is insufficient: $T(x)=x^2$ maps zero to zero and is still nonlinear. One failed pair of inputs disproves linearity; checking a few successful examples cannot prove a universal claim.

sections.heading: Columns are the images of the coordinate basis
sections.body: Write $x=x_1e_1+\cdots+x_ne_n$. If $T$ is linear, then $T(x)=x_1T(e_1)+\cdots+x_nT(e_n)$. Consequently the standard matrix is $A=[T(e_1)\ \cdots\ T(e_n)]$, with basis images as columns, not rows. Its shape is $m\times n$. This also proves that specifying the images of a basis determines a unique linear map. For a different input basis, first find the input's coefficients in that basis rather than treating those coefficients as standard coordinates.

sections.heading: Composition, kernel, and image
sections.body: If $S(x)=Ax$ and $T(y)=By$, then applying $S$ first and $T$ second gives $(T\circ S)(x)=B(Ax)=(BA)x$. The rightmost factor acts first. The kernel consists of inputs sent to zero, while the image consists of all reachable outputs and equals the span of the matrix columns. An injective map has zero kernel. A nontrivial kernel means distinct inputs can share an output because $T(x+k)=T(x)$ whenever $k$ is in the kernel.

worked_examples.prompt: A linear map satisfies $T(e_1)=(2,-1)$ and $T(e_2)=(3,4)$. Find its matrix and $T(2,-1)$.
steps: Place the images in columns to get $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}$.
The row-column product $A(2,-1)$ gives the same output.

worked_examples.prompt: Find the kernel and image of $T(x,y)=(x+2y,2x+4y)$.
steps: Factor the output as $(x+2y)(1,2)$, so every output lies on the line spanned by $(1,2)$.
Every multiple of $(1,2)$ is reached by setting $y=0$ and choosing $x$ freely.
To get zero, solve $x+2y=0$. Setting $y=t$ gives $(x,y)=t(-2,1)$.
The nonzero kernel vector $(-2,1)$ shows that the map is not injective.

questions.prompt: A linear map has $T(e_1)=(1,3)$ and $T(e_2)=(-2,4)$. Give its standard matrix.
questions.solution: $A=[T(e_1)\ T(e_2)]=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.concept: Constructing a matrix from basis images

questions.prompt: For a linear map with $T(e_1)=(1,3)$ and $T(e_2)=(-2,4)$, compute $T(3,-2)$.
Which map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is linear?
hints: A matrix times $(x,y)$ gives linear coordinate expressions with no constant term.
A product or square of input coordinates generally violates additivity.
questions.solution: The selected map is multiplication by $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$, hence linear. The translation fails at zero, the square fails homogeneity, and the product term fails additivity.

questions.prompt: Let $S(x,y)=(x+y,y)$ and $T(x,y)=(2x,3y)$. Compute $(T\circ S)(1,2)$.
questions.solution: First $S(1,2)=(3,2)$. Then $T(3,2)=(6,6)$. Reversing the maps would instead give $(8,6)$.

questions.prompt: The map $T(x,y)=(x+2y,2x+4y)$ sends $(k,3)$ to zero. Find $k$.
questions.solution: $k+2(3)=0$ gives $k=-6$. The second coordinate is then $2(-6)+4(3)=0$ too.

questions.prompt: Which description is the image of $T(x,y)=(x+2y,2x+4y)$?
hints: The second output coordinate is twice the first.
Every real first coordinate is reachable by choosing $y=0$.
questions.solution: Set $t=x+2y$. Then $T(x,y)=(t,2t)$. Conversely, choosing $(x,y)=(t,0)$ reaches every point of that line.

questions.prompt: Order the steps proving that the columns of a linear map's standard matrix are $T(e_i)$.
choices: The expression is the matrix-vector product for the matrix with columns $T(e_i)$.
Expand $x=\sum_i x_ie_i$ in the standard basis.
Conclude that this matrix represents $T$ on every input.
hints: Identify a column combination only after invoking linearity.
questions.solution: Write the basis expansion, apply linearity, recognize the column combination as matrix multiplication, and conclude equality on all inputs. The sequence is $2,3,1,4$.
questions.concept: Proof of the basis-image matrix rule

questions.prompt: Why does $F(x,y)=(x^2,y)$ disprove the claim that $F(0)=0$ alone implies linearity?
hints: Find a specific failure of homogeneity.
Compare scaling before and after applying the map.
questions.solution: Homogeneity would require $F(2(1,0))=2F(1,0)$. The two sides are $(4,0)$ and $(2,0)$, so $F$ is nonlinear despite preserving zero.
questions.concept: Counterexample to a false linearity test

questions.prompt: $S(x,y)=(x+2y,y)$ and $T(x,y)=(-y,x)$. Find the matrix for $T\circ S$.
hints: Alternatively multiply the matrix of $T$ on the left of the matrix of $S$.
questions.solution: $(T\circ S)(x,y)=(-y,x+2y)$, so the coefficients form $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: A linear map satisfies $T(1,1)=(3,1)$ and $T(1,-1)=(1,5)$. Find $T(3,1)$.
questions.concept: Linearity with a nonstandard input basis

lessons.title: Rotations, reflections, projections, and shears
lessons.summary: Recognize common plane transformations by their matrices, fixed vectors, inverses, and effects on lengths and areas.
objectives: Apply and construct rotation, reflection, projection, and shear matrices in the plane.
Distinguish invertible length-preserving maps from projections and shears.
Use composition and fixed-vector tests to interpret geometric transformations.

sections.heading: Rotations and reflections preserve Euclidean length
sections.body: A counterclockwise rotation through angle $\theta$ has matrix $R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Its columns are the rotated basis vectors. Reflection in the $x$-axis sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,-y)$, while reflection in the line $y=x$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(y,x)$. These matrices satisfy $Q^TQ=I$, so $\|Qv\|^2=v^TQ^TQv=\|v\|^2$. A rotation has determinant $1$; a reflection has determinant $-1$, reversing orientation.

sections.heading: Projection deliberately discards information
sections.body: Orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by a nonzero vector $a$ is $Pv=(aa^T/(a^Ta))v$. A projected vector lies on the target line and its residual is perpendicular to it. Projection is idempotent: $P^2=P$, because a vector already on the line stays unchanged. A plane-to-line projection has a nonzero kernel and is not invertible; lost perpendicular components cannot be reconstructed from the output. The identity $P^T=P$ distinguishes orthogonal projections from general oblique projections.

sections.heading: Shears preserve area but can change length
sections.body: A horizontal shear $H_k=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(x+ky,y)$ and fixes every point on the $x$-axis. Its determinant is $1$, so it preserves signed area, but $H_k(0,1)=(k,1)$ usually has length greater than one. Its inverse is $H_{-k}$, which subtracts the same horizontal shift. Geometric maps need not commute: rotating a sheared vector generally differs from shearing a rotated vector. To identify a composition, follow a test vector through the rightmost transformation first.

worked_examples.prompt: Rotate $(2,-1)$ counterclockwise by $90$ degrees, then reflect in the $x$-axis.
steps: A $90$-degree counterclockwise rotation sends $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$, giving $(1,2)$.
Reflection in the $x$-axis changes only the sign of the second coordinate, giving $(1,-2)$.
The original and final squared lengths are both $5$, as expected for a composition of orthogonal maps.

worked_examples.prompt: Construct the orthogonal projection matrix onto the line spanned by $(1,2)$ and apply it to $(5,0)$.
steps: The residual $(4,-2)$ has dot product $4-4=0$ with $(1,2)$, and projecting $(1,2)$ again leaves it unchanged.

questions.prompt: Rotate $(3,-2)$ counterclockwise by $90$ degrees.
hints: Preserve the original length as a check.
questions.solution: $R_{90}(3,-2)=(-(-2),3)=(2,3)$. Both vectors have squared length $13$.

questions.prompt: Reflect $(-4,7)$ across the line $y=x$.
hints: It does not negate either coordinate.
questions.solution: The reflection matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so the output is $(7,-4)$.

questions.prompt: Project $(4,-3)$ orthogonally onto the $x$-axis.
hints: The target line has second coordinate zero.
An orthogonal projection keeps the parallel component.
questions.solution: Projection onto the $x$-axis has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, giving $(4,0)$. The residual $(0,-3)$ is perpendicular to the axis.

questions.prompt: Apply the horizontal shear $H_3(x,y)=(x+3y,y)$ to $(-1,2)$.
hints: Add three times the vertical coordinate to the horizontal one.
questions.solution: A horizontal shear leaves the second coordinate unchanged and adds three times that coordinate to the first. Thus $H_3(-1,2)=(-1+3(2),2)=(5,2)$. The vertical height remains $2$ while the point moves six units to the right.

questions.prompt: Give the inverse matrix of $H_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
hints: The vertical coordinate still stays fixed.
questions.solution: $H_2^{-1}=H_{-2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplication in either order cancels the upper-right entry and produces the identity.

questions.prompt: Find the orthogonal projection matrix onto the line $y=x$.
questions.solution: $aa^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $a^Ta=2$, so $P=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.concept: Projection matrix from a direction vector

questions.prompt: Which property distinguishes a nontrivial horizontal shear from a rotation?
choices: It can change a vector's Euclidean length.
questions.answer: It can change a vector's Euclidean length.
hints: Both maps are invertible linear maps with determinant one.
Compare the norm of $(0,1)$ before and after shearing.
questions.solution: For $k\ne0$, $H_k(0,1)=(k,1)$ has length $\sqrt{k^2+1}>1$. Rotations preserve all lengths. The other listed properties hold for both.

questions.prompt: Order the steps proving $P^2=P$ for the projection $P=aa^T/(a^Ta)$ with $a\ne0$.
choices: Since $a\ne0$, $a^Ta>0$, so the cancellation is valid.
hints: Expand the square before grouping the middle factors.
Check the denominator is nonzero before canceling.
questions.solution: Substitute the formula, regroup the middle $a^Ta$ as a scalar, establish positivity, then cancel one copy. One valid order is $2,3,4,1$. Positivity may also be established before substitution or before regrouping; these valid orderings are accepted too.

questions.prompt: First apply $H_2(x,y)=(x+2y,y)$ to $(1,3)$, then rotate counterclockwise by $90$ degrees. Give the final vector.
questions.solution: $H_2(1,3)=(7,3)$ and $R_{90}(7,3)=(-3,7)$. In the reversed order the output would be $( -1,1)$, so order matters.

questions.prompt: Let $P$ be orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by $(1,2)$. Which nonzero input is sent to zero?
hints: Projection kills vectors perpendicular to its target line.
Find the option whose dot product with $(1,2)$ is zero.
questions.solution: $(2,-1)\cdot(1,2)=2-2=0$, so its projection coefficient is zero. The other listed vectors have nonzero dot products with the target direction.

lessons.title: Affine versus linear maps
lessons.summary: Separate a linear transformation from a translation and understand why affine maps preserve weighted points whose coefficients sum to one.
objectives: Identify the matrix and translation in an affine map $F(x)=Ax+b$.
Test whether an affine map is linear and compute affine compositions and inverses.
Prove preservation of affine combinations and explain homogeneous coordinates.

sections.heading: Translations move the origin
sections.body: An affine map has the form $F(x)=Ax+b$, where $A$ is a matrix and $b$ is a fixed vector in the output space. Its value at the origin is $b$. It is linear exactly when $b=0$: every matrix map is linear, while a nonzero translation violates $F(0)=0$. The change between two outputs is still linear, since $F(x)-F(y)=A(x-y)$. Thus affine maps transform displacement vectors using $A$ even when point coordinates include a translation.

sections.heading: Affine combinations preserve the sum of weights
sections.body: For coefficients satisfying $\sum_i c_i=1$, one has $F(\sum_i c_ix_i)=\sum_i c_iF(x_i)$. Expanding the right side gives $A\sum_i c_ix_i+b\sum_i c_i$, and the weight condition leaves exactly one copy of $b$. Midpoints use weights $1/2,1/2$, so affine maps preserve midpoints. Convex combinations additionally require nonnegative weights and describe line segments and convex sets. Arbitrary linear combinations are not preserved when $b\ne0$.

sections.heading: Composition and inverse keep the affine form
sections.body: If $F(x)=Ax+b$ and $G(y)=Cy+d$, then $(G\circ F)(x)=CAx+Cb+d$. Notice that the second map transforms the first translation. If $A$ is invertible, solve $y=Ax+b$ to obtain $F^{-1}(y)=A^{-1}(y-b)$. In homogeneous coordinates, a point $x$ is represented as $(x,1)$ and the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ represents the affine map. A displacement uses last coordinate zero, so the translation column contributes nothing to it.

worked_examples.prompt: For $F(x,y)=(2x-y+3,x+y-2)$, identify $A,b$ and decide whether $F$ is linear.
steps: Evaluate the origin: $F(0,0)=(3,-2)\ne(0,0)$, so the map is affine but not linear.
For $u=(1,2)$ and $v=(0,1)$, $F(u)-F(v)=A(u-v)=A(1,1)=(1,2)$; translations cancel in differences.
worked_examples.result: $F(x)=Ax+b$ with nonzero $b$, so it is not linear.

worked_examples.prompt: Let $F(x,y)=(x+2,y-1)$ and $G(x,y)=(2x,-y)$. Compute $G\circ F$ and its inverse.
steps: Substitution into the composite returns $(u,v)$, verifying the inverse.

questions.prompt: Which map is affine but not linear?
hints: An affine coordinate formula has constant plus linear terms.
A nonzero constant vector prevents linearity.
questions.solution: The selected map is $Ix+(3,-1)$, so it is affine and moves zero. The first option is linear; the other two contain nonlinear input products.

questions.prompt: For $F(x,y)=(2x-y+4,3y-2)$, find the translation vector $b$.
hints: Set every input coordinate to zero.
questions.solution: $F(0,0)=(4,-2)$, so $b=(4,-2)$ and $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.prompt: For $F(x,y)=(2x+1,y-3)$, compute $F(4,2)$.
hints: Apply the linear part before adding constants.
The two output coordinates are $2(4)+1$ and $2-3$.
questions.solution: Direct substitution gives $F(4,2)=(8+1,2-3)=(9,-1)$.

questions.prompt: For what value of $k$ is $F(x,y)=(x+ky,2y+k)$ linear?
hints: The term $ky$ is linear for every fixed $k$; the constant $k$ in the second coordinate is the issue.
questions.solution: $F(0,0)=(0,k)$, so linearity requires $k=0$. For this value the map is $(x,2y)$, which is linear.

questions.concept: Affine maps act linearly on displacements

questions.prompt: Find the preimage of $(11,5)$ under $F(x,y)=(2x+3,y-4)$.
hints: Solve the two output equations separately.

questions.prompt: Order the steps proving an affine map $F(x)=Ax+b$ preserves midpoints.
hints: Start by evaluating $F$ at the midpoint.
Split the one translation into two halves only after expanding $A$.
questions.solution: Evaluate at the midpoint, distribute the linear part, combine $b$ into the numerator as two copies, then recognize $F(u)$ and $F(v)$. The order is $2,4,1,3$.

questions.prompt: Give the $3\times3$ homogeneous-coordinate matrix for $F(x,y)=(2x+y+3,-y+4)$ acting on $(x,y,1)$.
hints: Put the $2\times2$ linear part in the upper-left block.
The final column is the translation followed by a final $1$.
questions.solution: The required matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&-1&4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplying $(x,y,1)$ produces $(2x+y+3,-y+4,1)$.

questions.prompt: Let $F(x,y)=(x+1,2y-3)$ and $G(x,y)=(3x,y+4)$. Find $(G\circ F)(2,5)$.
questions.solution: $F(2,5)=(3,7)$ and $G(3,7)=(9,11)$. The composite formula is $(3x+3,2y+1)$.

questions.prompt: For $F(x)=Ax+b$ with $b\ne0$, which condition on $\alpha,\beta$ guarantees $F(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha F(u)+\beta F(v)$ for every $u,v$?
choices: $\alpha=\beta$, with no restriction on their common value
hints: Expand both sides and compare the coefficient of $b$.
The left side contains exactly one copy of the translation.
questions.solution: The right side is $A(\alpha u+\beta v)+(\alpha+\beta)b$, whereas the left side contains $+b$. Since $b\ne0$, equality for every input holds exactly when $\alpha+\beta=1$.
questions.concept: Affine combinations and weights summing to one
